summary: Defines a common terminology for GMPLS-based recovery mechanisms, meaning protection and restoration. The terminology does not depend on the underlying transport technology. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4427 gives network engineers common terms for describing how a Generalized MPLS path recovers from a failure. It defines the vocabulary for backup paths, traffic switching, and recovery timing, without specifying a protocol.

questions: what is the difference between protection and restoration
subtitle: Shared terminology for recovery of GMPLS label-switched paths.

tldr.problem: GMPLS recovery discussions used inconsistent terms for protection, restoration, traffic, switching, and timing.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a shared vocabulary for recovery paths, recovery types, participating functions, recovery phases, and timing measures.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational terminology document. It defines no recovery protocol or procedure for a particular implementation.

today: RFC 4427 is an Informational document published in March 2006. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the document defines terminology, not a protocol.

sections.title: Scope of the Recovery Vocabulary
sections.content:
RFC 4427 defines terminology for recovery of label-switched paths (LSPs) controlled by Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching (GMPLS). Here, recovery includes both protection and restoration. The terms apply across transport technologies and cover span, segment, and end-to-end recovery.

Recovery of the control plane itself is outside the document's scope. A working path and its recovery path are typically resource-disjoint so that one failure does not affect both.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC defines words for discussing backup behavior on GMPLS paths. It covers links, path segments, and complete paths, but not recovery of the control system.

sections.title: Working Paths, Traffic, and Recovery
sections.content:
A working LSP carries normal user traffic. A recovery LSP carries that traffic when the working path fails, and it may carry extra traffic while it is idle. Extra traffic can be pre-empted when recovery resources are needed; null traffic is ignored at the recovery path's egress.

Protection means the recovery path has been fully computed, signaled, and cross-connected before a failure. Restoration may reserve or signal some resources in advance, but completes path establishment after the failure. Recovery can cover a link span, part of a path, or the full path.
sections.plainLanguage: A working path carries normal traffic, while a recovery path carries it after a failure. Protection prepares the full spare path in advance; restoration completes more of the path after a failure.

sections.title: Recovery Types and Switching Functions
sections.content:
The recovery type describes how many recovery paths serve how many working paths. In 1+1 protection, one dedicated path protects one working path and receives a permanent copy of normal traffic. In 1:1, traffic uses one path at a time and the recovery path may carry extra traffic. In 1:N, one recovery path serves up to N working paths; in M:N, M recovery paths serve up to N working paths.

A bridge connects traffic to working or recovery paths. A selector chooses which path's normal traffic reaches the egress. Shared recovery can protect only one or M failed working paths at once, respectively.
sections.plainLanguage: The labels describe how backup capacity is assigned to working paths. A bridge connects traffic to paths, and a selector chooses which path supplies the normal traffic.

sections.title: Failure Phases and Recovery Timing
sections.content:
The RFC names five phases: detect the failure, locate and isolate it, notify the relevant entities, recover the path, and revert to normal operation when appropriate. Detection is the only phase the control plane cannot perform by itself. Detection, localization, and notification together form fault management.

It also defines detection, correlation, notification, and recovery-switching times. Their sum is total recovery time. Wait-to-restore time is the period after a fault is recovered before the LSP or span can be used again for normal traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Recovery starts by detecting and locating a failure, then notifying the decision makers and switching traffic. The RFC gives names to each phase and to the time spent in them.

sections.title: Protection and Restoration Schemes
sections.content:
The protection schemes include 1+1, 1:N, and M:N. The restoration schemes include pre-planned rerouting, where resources may be prepared but are not cross-connected, and full LSP rerouting, where the alternate path is established after failure. Shared-mesh restoration lets restoration paths from different ingress nodes share resources.

Hard restoration releases the old LSP before the replacement is fully established. Soft restoration releases it after the replacement is established. The RFC directs readers to RFC 4426 and RFC 4428 for functional and security details.
sections.plainLanguage: Protection reserves and connects recovery paths before a failure. Restoration establishes the replacement after a failure, and can release the old path either before or after the new one is ready.
